files.lesson.md: --- order: 3 unit: parallel node: AC9M7M04 n3 title: Reasoning with angles summary: "Find unknown angles in steps, giving a reason for each: what you know, the rule that links it to the next angle, and the reason in words. Parallel-line rules join straight-line and vertically opposite angles." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A detective does not guess: every step has evidence. Finding an angle is the same. Each angle you find needs a reason, and the reasons are what make the answer trustworthy." connection: stair-stringer app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8171 url: http://127.0.0.1:8171/index.html readySelector: ".pangles" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: lines.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$b = 70^\\circ$. Then $f = 70^\\circ$ (corresponding to $b$) and $h = 110^\\circ$ ($f$ and $h$ are on a straight line)." } explainClip: query: { code: "@lines.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "One step at a time, each with a reason" say: "Find angles one step at a time, with a reason for each." clip: - caption: { text: "b = 70°. Step 1: f = 70°, corresponding to b.", say: "Step one: f is corresponding to b, so seventy degrees." } - click: "Angle b, 70°" - click: "Angle f, 70°" - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "Step 2: h = 180° − 70° = 110°, on a straight line with f.", say: "Step two: h and f make a straight line, so one hundred and ten." } - click: "Angle b, 70°" - click: "Angle h, 110°" - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "straight line" } - wait: 1200 --- You know the rules: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$, and from Year 6, vertically opposite angles are equal and angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. Most problems need more than one rule. So you'll find angles **in steps**, and say which rule you used at each one. Write your working your own way: short notes are fine. The checker marks your answer and the reason at the step that matters; you compare the rest with a model. ## Predict: two steps ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to h when only b is known shows whether they look for a chain (b to f to h) or assume a link between b and h." check: type: predict q: "Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. $b = 70^\\circ$. What is $h$?" options: - "$110^\\circ$" - "$70^\\circ$" - "$20^\\circ$" - "$250^\\circ$" actual: "110°. b and h are not a named pair, so it takes two steps: f = 70° (corresponding to b), then h = 180° − 70° = 110° (f and h are on a straight line)." ``` $b$ and $h$ are not one of the pairs. Which angle could you find first? ## Run: check the chain ```step stage: run insight: "Setting b to 70° and comparing h shows the two-step answer, and turning the line shows h is always 180° minus b: the chain works for every angle." try: { playground: board, starter: "lines.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Turn the crossing line until $b = 70^\\circ$, then pick $b$ and $h$. Was your prediction right?", when: "b = 70 and u = 2 and v = 8" } ``` Then turn the crossing line. Is $h$ always $180^\circ - b$? Which two rules make that true? ## Investigate: reasons for every step ```step stage: investigate insight: "Know, choose the rule, state the reason: each step links an angle you know to the next by a named rule. Kai's mistake links two angles that only look related." tasks: - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-b, caption: "Two parallel lines. $b = 70^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $h$. Write each step with its reason." steps: - ["$f = 70^\\circ$", "corresponding to $b$: corresponding angles are equal"] - ["$h = 180^\\circ - 70^\\circ = 110^\\circ$", "$f$ and $h$ are on a straight line"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Corresponding angles are equal", "Alternate angles are equal", "Co-interior angles add to 180°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are between the lines. b is above the top line.", "b and f are not between the lines, and they are equal, not adding to 180°."] answer: "110" feedback: - ["70", "h is not in the same place as b. Find f first, then look at f and h."] explain: "f = 70° (corresponding to b), h = 110° (a straight line with f). Another route: d = 110° (a straight line with b), h = 110° (corresponding to d)." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kai" text: "Kai finds $e$ when $b = 70^\\circ$. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: assume-equal-angles explain: "Line 2: b and e are not a named pair (b is above the top line, e above the bottom line, on different sides). Looking related is not a reason. e = 110°: f = 70° (corresponding to b), then e = 180° − 70° (a straight line)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-d, caption: "Two parallel lines. $d = 115^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $g$. Write each step with its reason." steps: - ["$e = 115^\\circ$", "alternate to $d$: alternate angles are equal"] - ["$g = 180^\\circ - 115^\\circ = 65^\\circ$", "$e$ and $g$ are on a straight line"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Alternate angles are equal", "Corresponding angles are equal", "Co-interior angles add to 180°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "d and e are not in the same place at each crossing.", "d and e are on opposite sides of the crossing line."] answer: "65" feedback: - ["115", "g is not alternate to d. Find e first."] explain: "e = 115° (alternate to d), g = 65° (a straight line with e). Or: f = 65° (co-interior with d), g = 65° (vertically opposite f)." ``` ### Know, choose, say why Here is the routine for every step: what you know, the rule that links it to a new angle, and the reason. ```worked b = 70^\circ :: Know: the given angle. f = 70^\circ :: Choose: $f$ is in the same place as $b$ at the other crossing. Say why: corresponding angles are equal. h = 180^\circ - 70^\circ :: Choose: $h$ is next to $f$ on the bottom line. Say why: angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. h = 110^\circ :: Done: two steps, two reasons. ``` Now find $h$ yourself. Write it your own way; the checker marks your answer and the reason for the first step, then shows you a model to compare. ### Find the mistake Read Kai's reasoning one line at a time. Which step has no real rule behind it? ### Another chain ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a different starting angle, a different route, the reverse direction, then lines that are not parallel and showing lines are parallel from the angles." try: { playground: board, starter: "lines.yml#converse", height: 560 } tasks: - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-a, caption: "Two parallel lines. $a = 130^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $f$, with a reason for each step." steps: - ["$e = 130^\\circ$", "corresponding to $a$"] - ["$f = 180^\\circ - 130^\\circ = 50^\\circ$", "$e$ and $f$ are on a straight line"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["Angles on a straight line add to 180°", "Co-interior angles add to 180°", "Vertically opposite angles are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "e and f are at the same crossing, so they are not co-interior.", "e and f are next to each other, not opposite."] answer: "50" feedback: - ["130", "f is not in the same place as a."] explain: "e = 130° (corresponding to a), f = 50° (a straight line with e). Or b = 50° (a straight line with a), f = 50° (corresponding to b)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-e, caption: "Two parallel lines. $e = 140^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $b$, going up from the bottom line." steps: - ["$c = 180^\\circ - 140^\\circ = 40^\\circ$", "co-interior with $e$: co-interior angles add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$b = 40^\\circ$", "vertically opposite $c$"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Co-interior angles add to 180°", "Alternate angles are equal", "Corresponding angles are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "c and e are on the same side of the crossing line.", "c and e are not in the same place at each crossing."] answer: "40" feedback: - ["140", "b is not equal to e. Try c first: it is between the lines with e."] explain: "c = 40° (co-interior with e), b = 40° (vertically opposite c)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-h, caption: "Two parallel lines. $h = 125^\\circ$." } check: type: answer q: "Find $c$. (Use your own steps; two are enough.)" answer: "55" feedback: - ["125", "c is not in the same place as h, and not alternate to it."] explain: "d = 125° (corresponding to h), then c = 55° (a straight line with d)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#tilt-pic, caption: "$c = 60^\\circ$, $f = 45^\\circ$. No arrows on the lines." } check: type: question q: "Are these two lines parallel?" options: ["No: c and f are alternate angles, but they are not equal", "Yes: c and f are alternate angles", "You cannot tell from angles"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are equal only when the lines are parallel. These are not equal.", "You can: if the lines were parallel, c and f would be equal."] explain: "If the lines were parallel, the alternate angles c and f would be equal. They are not, so the lines are not parallel." - starter: "lines.yml#converse" hint: ["Change w, the tilt of the lower line.", "Stop when c and f are equal."] check: { type: board, text: "Backwards: tilt the lower line until the alternate angles $c$ and $f$ are equal. What does that tell you about the lines?", when: "c = f", explain: "When alternate angles are equal, the lines are parallel (w = 0). Equal corresponding or alternate angles, or co-interior angles adding to 180°, show that lines are parallel." } ``` ### A different start Each task changes one thing. Your working is yours; the marked parts are the answer and one reason. ### Up from the bottom ### Your own route ### Not parallel ### Showing lines are parallel ## Practise: angle chains ```step stage: practise insight: "Two-step chains with each rule, mixed, with a reason named every time; the review keeps the pair names apart from vertically opposite angles." tasks: - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-g, caption: "Two parallel lines. $g = 75^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $a$, with a reason for each step." steps: - ["$c = 75^\\circ$", "corresponding to $g$"] - ["$a = 180^\\circ - 75^\\circ = 105^\\circ$", "$a$ and $c$ are on a straight line"] answer: "105" feedback: - ["75", "a is not in the same place as g."] explain: "c = 75° (corresponding to g), a = 105° (a straight line with c)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-c, caption: "Two parallel lines. $c = 80^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $h$, with a reason for each step." steps: - ["$e = 180^\\circ - 80^\\circ = 100^\\circ$", "co-interior with $c$"] - ["$h = 100^\\circ$", "vertically opposite $e$"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Co-interior angles add to 180°", "Co-interior angles are equal", "Alternate angles are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Co-interior angles add to 180°: they are equal only when both are 90°.", "c and e are on the same side, so they are not alternate."] answer: "100" feedback: - ["80", "Check your first step: c and e are co-interior."] explain: "e = 100° (co-interior with c), h = 100° (vertically opposite e). Or g = 80° (corresponding to c), h = 100° (a straight line with g)." - picture: { ref: lines.yml#given-b, caption: "Two parallel lines. $b = 70^\\circ$." } check: type: question q: "Review: Tom says \"$b$ and $c$ are alternate angles\". Which is right?" options: ["They are vertically opposite: both at the top crossing", "Tom is right", "They are corresponding"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are one at each crossing, between the lines.", "Corresponding angles are one at each crossing."] explain: "b and c are at the same crossing, opposite each other: vertically opposite (and equal for that reason)." ``` ### Down the page ### Through the middle ### Review: one crossing ## Make: set it up ```step stage: make insight: "Working backwards from a target angle two steps away, then checking on the board, reverses the chain: reasoning first, the board only confirms." try: { playground: board, starter: "lines.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["h and f are on a straight line, so f = 180° − 125°.", "b is corresponding to f."] check: { type: board, text: "Work out what $b$ must be for $h = 125^\\circ$. Then turn the crossing line until $b$ is that size: only $b$ is shown, and this ticks when $h = 125^\\circ$.", when: "h = 125", explain: "f = 55° (a straight line with h), so b = 55° (corresponding to f)." } ``` Write your two steps first, then turn the line. Stretch: write your own two-step puzzle for a partner: give one angle, ask for one that is not a named pair with it, and write the model reasons. ## Make: a stair cut, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A stair stringer makes the treads two parallel lines and the sloping edge a transversal; the cut needs a two-step chain with a reason at each step." hint: ["Find the angle next to the one you know first. What is the reason?", "The treads are parallel. Which pair of angles is in the same place at each crossing?"] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "On a stair stringer, two treads are level, parallel lines. The sloping edge crosses them. At the lower tread, the angle above the line on the right of the edge is 38°. What is the angle above the upper tread, on the left of the edge?" steps: - ["Sketch two level lines crossed by the sloping edge, with 38° above the lower line on the right", "the 38° is made up for the task"] - ["The angle above the lower line on the left makes a straight line with 38°: 180° − 38° = 142°", "angles on a straight line add to 180°"] - ["The angle above the upper line on the left is in the same place at the upper crossing, so it is also 142°", "corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Why is the angle at the upper tread 142°?" options: - "It is in the same place at the other crossing, and the treads are parallel" - "It is vertically opposite the 38° angle" - "It is alternate to the 38° angle" - "The two angles are co-interior, so they are equal" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Vertically opposite angles are at one crossing. These are at two.", "Alternate angles lie between the lines, on opposite sides. This one is above the upper line.", "Co-interior angles add to 180° and are not equal in general."] answer: "142" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["38", "That is the angle you were given. The one you want is next to it on a straight line, then copied up to the next tread."] - ["52", "That is 90° − 38°. The treads are parallel, not at right angles to the edge."] criteria: - "I sketched two level lines and the sloping edge, and marked the 38°." - "I gave a reason for each step: a straight line, then corresponding angles." - "I checked that 142° and 38° make a straight line together." explain: "180° − 38° = 142° on the lower tread (a straight line), then the same place at the upper tread is also 142° (corresponding angles, because the treads are parallel)." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Sketch the treads and the edge, write each step with its reason, then type the angle. The 38° is made up for the task: a real stair's pitch comes from the building rules. **Also used in** - **Carpentry.** A carpenter marks every tread cut from one angle, because the treads are parallel. - **Periscopes.** Two parallel mirrors give equal angles that keep the view level: [Finding angles with parallel lines](../parallel-angles/). ```teacher summary: Students find unknown angles at parallel lines in two-step chains, with a reason for each step, writing their working their own way; the platform marks the answer and the reason at the key step, then shows a model to compare with (AC9M7M04, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find an unknown angle in two or more steps, using parallel-line, straight-line and vertically opposite angles. - I can give a reason for each step, naming the rule. - I can use angles to show whether two lines are parallel. struggle: "Choosing which angle to find first. Ask: which angle can you get from the one you know in one step, and what is the reason?" before: > Do the first reasoning task yourself first, then compare with its model. Students need both parallel-lines lessons and Year 6 angle facts (straight line, vertically opposite, at a point). The one idea: know, choose the rule, say why. Every angle found needs a named reason. The common mistake is linking two angles that only look related (Kai's b and e); it is planted after the routine. The reasoning tasks do not mark the free working: students write it their own way (notes, abbreviations such as "vert. opp." and "co-int." are fine). The answer is marked, and at one key step students choose the reason from a list, so the misconception gets feedback. Then they compare their working with a model and tick a short self-check. Look at the working in class: it is where reasoning shows. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 70° are assuming b and h are linked directly." - "Run: ask students to say the two rules that make h = 180° − b true for every crossing angle." - "Investigate: model know, choose, say why on the board, writing the reason in short form. Accept any correct route." - "Modify: collect two different routes to f and ask which is shorter." - "Make: ask students to say their two steps before they turn the line." - "Make on paper: ask for the reason at each line before anyone types an answer." stuck: - see: A student links two angles that only look related (Kai's mistake). ask: Which rule links them? Name it. fix: If no rule links them directly, find an angle in between that does. - see: A student gets the right angle with no reasons. ask: How would you convince someone who did not see the diagram? fix: "Write one reason per line: the angle, then why." - see: A student cannot find a first step. ask: Which angles can you find straight from the given one? fix: List every angle one rule away from the given one; the target is usually among those, or one more step on. stretch: "Write a three-step puzzle for a partner: give one angle, ask for an angle three rules away, and write the model reasons." support: "Allow the Run board for checking each step: set the given angle, pick pairs and read the names." leads: > Next: angle sums of triangles and polygons, then Unknown angles in shapes, which combines them with these rules. Where it leads: geometric proof (Years 8 to 10), where a chain of reasons is the proof. exit: q: A transversal crosses two parallel lines, making a 120° angle. Find the angle alternate to it and the angle co-interior to it, with reasons. a: 120° (alternate angles are equal) and 180° − 120° = 60° (co-interior angles add to 180°). explain: > Most angle problems take more than one step. For each step: 1. **Know**: an angle you already have. 2. **Choose**: a rule that links it to a new angle: corresponding or alternate angles are equal, co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$, vertically opposite angles are equal, angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. 3. **Say why**: write the rule as the reason. $b = 70^\circ$: $f = 70^\circ$ (corresponding to $b$), then $h = 110^\circ$ ($f$ and $h$ are on a straight line). If two angles only look related, find one in between that a rule links to both. ```
